newsitem.title: GERMANY: German leaders see no chance of costly EU job deal.
newsitem.headline: German leaders see no chance of costly EU job deal.

text.p: German political leaders said on Sunday they were firmly opposed to French proposals for a costly drive to make jobs for Europe's 18 million unemployed.

Finance Minister Theo Waigel, Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel and Chancellor Helmut Kohl's top deputy Wolfgang Schaeuble all dismissed the French ideas as obsolete and said there was no chance Germany would agree to them at the European Union's summit in Amsterdam on Monday and Tuesday.

"We will stick to our position that there will be no money flowing from Germany for additional jobs creation programmes," Waigel told Reuters on the fringes of an official ceremony in the Bavarian town of Bad Woerishofen.
The summit, called to agree a new EU treaty, has been overshadowed by a rift between France and Germany over how to proceed toward monetary union.

EU countries hoped the summit would ratify a German-designed stability pact intended to impose discipline for the proposed single European currency by punishing nations failing to adhere to strict fiscal standards.
But France's new Socialist prime minister Lionel Jospin upset the plans by demanding last week that the 18 million jobless in the EU be taken into account.

Kohl, who met French leaders on Friday in an unsuccessful bid to reach agreement, ran into a stormy protest from 2,700 farmers who gathered outside the Bad Woerishofen ceremony on Sunday with banners reading "Farm Killer" and "Helmut Kohl Is To Germany What Mad Cow Disease Is To England".
"We are doing everything humanly possible in Brussels," Kohl told them. "A society without farmers would be a poor society."
Waigel told the Frankfurter Allgemeine Sonntagszeitung Bonn had ruled out participating.

"I will not go along with (state job creation programmes) under which Germany pays one third to Europe and gets only 15 percent back," Waigel told the newspaper. He expected some form of agreement on job strategies at the summit meeting but said this would not be tied in with additional spending.

Wolfgang Schaeuble, leader of Kohl's Christian Democrats in parliament, said most EU nations were on Germany's side in the dispute and said raising taxes and debt to finance jobs schemes had failed in the past and wouldn't work in the future.

"The problem of unemployment cannot be resolved with higher taxes or higher borrowing," Schaeuble told Der Spiegel newsweekly. "Deficit-spending to create new jobs and boost the economy is an obsolete economic theory."
Kinkel, in an interview with Welt am Sonntag newspaper, said there would be a chapter in the Amsterdam treaty on employment but there would not be any new spending for it.
"There will be no transfer from Germany of additional authorities to the EU and no additional funding," Kinkel said.

Edmund Stoiber, a leading conservative and well-known euro-sceptic turned up the volume on Sunday, saying the euro must be delayed if the stability targets are not met and warned politicians will lose public confidence if they trade the mark for a weaker currency.
The Bavarian premier said in an interview with Bild am Sonntag newspaper that replacing the mark with a weaker single European currency could harm German democracy.
"The overriding question for politicians and especially for the public at large is not when the euro will be introduced but rather whether it is a stable euro," Stoiber said.

"The mark is inseparably linked to our 'economic miracle'," Stoiber added. "And anyone who would replace the strong mark with a weaker euro and thus turn the currency conversion into a currency reform would destroy the public's confidence in politicians and damage democracy in Germany."

Stoiber's remarks came as a Forsa research institute survey found a slim majority of Germans against the euro. The survey of 1,011 Germans found that 51 percent opposed the euro's introduction while 34 percent were in favour.

The Bundesbank, meanwhile, denied a report in Der Spiegel claiming central bank president Hans Tietmeyer had urged the creation of a plan to ensure an orderly delay in monetary union. REUTER 151519 GMT jun 97
